g.text: Viz. of the pedestrian reality along Karl-Marx-Allee
Enrique Poza Herranz_2026_UdK_Ma Infodesign_Berlin
Stride, wander, stroll, trudge, go, move, step,
march, advance, pace, trek, hike, tread,
ramble, tramp, promenade, amble, saunter,
take a turn, traipse, toddle, make one's way,
mosey, plod, perambulate, footslog.
Collins Dictionary provides 26 synonyms for
"Walk"all variations of striding, but this project
ﬁlters them to a single deﬁnition: commuting,
or the movement from A to B over time.
The title references J.D. Salinger’s novel
The
Catcher in the Rye
. Holden the protagonist, asks
a taxi driver where ducks in Central Park, New
York City go when the lake freezes.
The driver replies, “They ﬂy away.”
In December 2025, as I moved to
Friedrichshain, I saw the desertic Karl-Marx-
Allee and asked myself the same question:
Where do people go when the city turns grey?
As every city transforms across seasons, this
project documents the winter-to-spring shift by
portraying the pedestrian reality.
To guide the project, two hypotheses were
derived from my own walking experience.
Lower temperature, higher speed. A negative
correlation where cold accelerates pedestrians.
Walk.A triangle of dependency where Walk
cannot be understood without the urban
context.
The built city and green spaces inﬂuence
behavior: large avenues with greenery slow
walkers; dense urban areas stresses them.
A mixed methodology combining open data and
self-gathered information was used.
Roads, buildings, and green areas came from
OpenStreetMap, while for self-gathered data was
collected through
Shadowing,
an anthropological
ﬁeldwork method based on non-participant
observation, in which individuals are followed to
systematically document their interactions with the
urban environment.

text.tspan: Target: Men between 20–40 years wearing dark

g.text: clothes and carrying a backpack.
Rules:
2. Starts from a public transport station.
3. Observer follows subject to destination.
4. If the case notices me, session ﬁnished.
5. Each case includes a photo.
6. Stops are recorded
Each session was recorded via Strava GPS tracking
app that logs, time, location, steps, pictures and
observations like weather and temperature.
The cartographic layer was designed in QGIS.
The research area is located in Friedrichshain
from Strausberger Platz along Karl-Marx-Allee
to Proskauer Straße. Vertically, it spans from
Ostbahnhof to Landsberger Allee. Resulting in
a huge area of 3,456,000m
To process these dimensions, a grid with
squares measuring 120m on each side was
crated, with a total of 20 squares length and 12
height.
The Strava cases were exported as CSVs to
QGIS. Where they can be visualized on the map
with their starting and ending point, pictures
and case number.
In a orange to black color gradient is visualized
the calculated average velocity (m/s). Slowest
(Black, 0.3 m/s) to fastest (Orange 2.07 m/s),
mean 1.438 m/s.
Finally, each layer were exported as SVGs and
composed in Aﬃnity.
After the design process, each hypothesis was
statistically tested using R to determine whether
it was supported by the data.
H1: Temperature–Walk.
Expected outcome, negative correlation:
colder = faster.
Of 47 cases, stop cases were excluded to
reduce noise, leaving a ﬁnal sample of 40 cases.
A Pearson correlation test between “grad” (°C)
and “vel” (velocity) yielded:
r
p
The positive
r
temperature = higher speed. However, the
result is not statistically signiﬁcant
p
Resulting H1 cannot be conﬁrmed or rejected;
a larger sample would be required to draw
conclusions.
Although the result is not statistically
signiﬁcant, the tendency shows that colder
weather slows the Walk.
H2: Urbanism–Nature–Walk.
The study area is divided by two architectural
typologies along a diagonal from Karl-Marx-Allee
through Friedenstraße (north) and
Marchlewskistraße (south).
This architectural dichotomy divides the city into
an eastern half characterized by a dense Altbau
development, narrow streets and ground-ﬂoor
commerces, in contrast to the western half with
big Soviet-style residential blocks and a city
planning with numerous green spaces.
To evaluate H2 each case was classiﬁed
according to its endpoint: E (east) or W (west).
This leads to sub-hypothesis H2.1: Which urban
environment attracts more pedestrians?
All cases were taken into account (stopping is
interpreted as a sign pleasure).
As with H1, R was used with the help of AI to
calculate the statistics. First the average speed of
each half was calculated and then a t-test
conducted.
Average speed:
E marked cases: 1.512 m/s
W marked cases: 1.280 m/s
t-test:

=0.030, Cohen’s

between W and W.
p
<0.05 conﬁrms statistical signiﬁcance.
And
d
≈0.8 is a high eﬀect size, providing
strong support for H2, not only in the data but
also in the practice.
Conclusion: H2 is conﬁrmed. Higher building
density and lower availability of green
spaces = higher pedestrian speed.
H2.1 Pedestrian density:
More target-proﬁle pedestrians in the
eastern area.
Where do the ducks go when the pond freezes?
is both a design project and a methodological
exercise. It introduced R, descriptive statistics,
and AI as a tool into my design workﬂow.
This project has been the convergence point
for many of my academic and professional
interests, including urban planning, social
sciences or design-led research. Where the
role of information design is particularly
noteworthy, as it is an indispensable tool for
organizing, categorizing and visualizing
diﬀerent types of data.
On of the major discoveries has been the
development of my own methodology, which
has enabled me to document a human reality.
Reaching that point was the greatest
challenge, as after that I just has to ﬁlter,
calculate and organize my data, based on my
two hypotheses.
Lastly my answer to Holden's queries: the ducks
do not disappear. We are here, moving through
the city, guided by free will but constrained by
the consequences of our actions.
And when the grey winter comes, at least try to
ﬂy away.
